title: Flash Flood Devastates Villages in Nepal's Gorkha, Bridges Swept Away as 10 Go Missing
excerpt: A sudden surge in the Budhi Gandaki river swept away settlements, six bridges and a hydropower project in Gorkha district; the army and helicopters have been deployed as 10 people remain missing.
body:
• A sudden flash flood swept through the Budhi Gandaki river basin in Nepal's Gorkha district on Sunday morning, destroying settlements, six bridges and a hydropower project.
  • At least 10 people are reported missing and around 35 houses were swept away in Painyu and Bagar villages, according to officials cited by ANI.
  • Nepal has deployed army units by air and land, rescue helicopters and a rapid response team from Kathmandu; six people have been evacuated to safer locations.
  • The disaster comes weeks after the August 26 Bhotekoshi-Trishuli floods that killed 1,455 people and left 5,285 missing.

Chilling footage circulating online shows the Budhi Gandaki river tearing through Gorkha district in northern Nepal on Sunday morning, swallowing entire stretches of Salleri Bazaar, levelling homes in Jagat Bazaar and carrying bridges, buildings and debris downstream.

The sudden surge in the river basin devastated settlements including Salleri, Jagat, Dovan and Ghattekhola. Preliminary reports cited by news agency ANI say around 35 houses were swept away in Painyu and Bagar in Ward 3 of Chumnubri Rural Municipality, and at least 10 people have been missing since the surge struck.

"Nepal has mobilised security personnel and helicopters to evacuate residents and provide relief in the affected region."

— The Times of India, reporting on the rescue operation

Bridges and infrastructure gone

The flooding destroyed or damaged six bridges, including motorable and suspension bridges, cutting off connections between several settlements. Bridges at Arughat, Tripurasundari and Soti-Manbu were among those swept away, assistant chief district officer Netra Prasad Sharma told ANI. A Bailey bridge linking wards 1 and 3 of Dharche Rural Municipality was also destroyed, and the flood damaged a hydropower project in the district.

https://x.com/MarioNawfal/status/2109202342692421640

Authorities have yet to establish what triggered the surge. Residents have raised the possibility that a blocked tributary or a landslide dam that suddenly gave way may have caused the flash flood — a mechanism that has caused deadly surges in Nepal's mountain rivers before.

Army, helicopters deployed

Prime Minister Balendra Shah said a Nepali Army contingent had been deployed by air and land for search and rescue operations, and a rapid response team from Kathmandu was airlifted to the area. The Nepal Army said six people had been evacuated to safer locations.

Home Minister Sudan Gurung urged people living along the Budhi Gandaki river to move to safer areas, warning that the river's flow continued to fluctuate. Police, the Armed Police Force and local authorities have been mobilised, while the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority has urged residents in vulnerable riverside settlements to relocate and remain alert, according to the Associated Press.

A country still reeling

The disaster lands while Nepal is still grappling with the aftermath of the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli floods on August 26, which killed 1,455 people and left 5,285 missing, devastating homes and infrastructure across mountainous areas. That tragedy left communities vulnerable to exactly the kind of secondary disaster unfolding in Gorkha — with damaged slopes, weakened banks and displaced populations facing fresh surges.

Diaspora angle

Nepal's diaspora — including the large Nepali community in the United States, the Gulf and Australia — will be anxiously checking on family in the affected districts. For Indians abroad too, Gorkha is familiar ground: it draws trekkers and pilgrims, and many Indian families have ties to the region. The Home Ministry's evacuation advisories remain in force for riverside settlements, and the full extent of the damage is still unclear.

What's next

Rescue teams are racing against time to reach cut-off villages and account for the missing. Investigators will examine whether a landslide dam or blocked tributary triggered the surge — findings that will matter for early-warning systems across Nepal's vulnerable river basins. More rain in the coming days could complicate the operation.
